content: Swine influenza, also known as swine flu, is an illness caused by any virus belonging to the Orthomyxoviridae family that is endemic to pig populations. Viruses that are endemic in swine are referred to as swine influenza viruses (SIV). All known strains of SIV are classified as either Influenza virus A, which is common, or Influenza virus C, which is rare. Influenza virus B has not been reported in swine. In humans, all three clades of influenza viruses—Influenza virus A, B, and C—are endemic. Individuals who work closely with poultry and swine, particularly those with significant exposure, are at risk of contracting infections from these animals if the animals carry a strain capable of infecting humans. SIV has the potential to mutate into a form that enables human-to-human transmission. The strain responsible for the 2009 swine flu outbreak is believed to have undergone such a mutation. In humans, the symptoms of swine flu closely resemble those of seasonal influenza and other influenza-like illnesses.
